summary: Horn argues that documented and foreseeable suffering supports apostolic sincerity; Paulogia answers that evidence for several named leaders cannot establish all eleven.

pro.text: they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus the Christ
pro.context: Horn quotes Acts to support collective, continuing proclamation by the apostles after authorities ordered them to stop.

con.text: there isn't strong evidence for that positive claim
con.context: Paulogia distinguishes evidence for sincere named leaders from the stronger claim that all eleven publicly persisted under danger.

moves.words: Horn narrows the traditional martyrdom claim, distinguishing strong evidence for several named leaders from weaker traditions about the remaining original apostles.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn materially improves the traditional argument by separating comparatively supported deaths and leadership risks from later, weaker traditions, explicitly concentrating confidence on Peter, Paul, James the brother of Jesus, and James son of Zebedee. Principal limitation: Those four cases still rest on different sources that establish unequal combinations of death, public proclamation, persecutor motive, recantation opportunity, and firsthand experience, so the narrowed category remains internally heterogeneous. Live burden: Horn must demonstrate the relevant sincerity-producing pathway for each named person before extending any inference to otherwise undocumented disciples, while Paulogia must engage the restricted cases rather than the abandoned universal legend. Locked score: 89 reflects excellent scope control and evidential discrimination, moderated because the strongest qualification also exposes how little uniform support remains for the wider apostolic conclusion.

moves.words: Paulogia grants that Horn’s restrained formulation improves on familiar church claims that every apostle certainly died after refusing an explicit opportunity to recant.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia fairly identifies Horn’s formulation as substantially more restrained than church narratives in which every apostle certainly faced execution, received an explicit recantation offer, and refused it, thereby clarifying the actual disagreement. Principal limitation: The autobiographical comparison establishes that a cruder popular argument is overstated but contributes little direct evidence about the narrower historical cases Horn actually defends. Live burden: Paulogia must assess the named leaders and collective texts on their own merits, while Horn must prevent acknowledgment of his nuance from functioning as agreement about undocumented preaching, danger, or endurance among the eleven. Locked score: 89 rewards unusually constructive framing, accurate concession, and dialectical fairness, with a modest deduction because this intervention reorganizes the target more effectively than it adjudicates the surviving evidence.

moves.words: Horn centers his strongest historical case on Peter, Paul, James the brother of Jesus, and James son of Zebedee rather than every later martyr tradition.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn creates a concrete evidential center by identifying Peter, Paul, James the brother of Jesus, and James son of Zebedee as better supported than the remaining disciples, grounding discussion in early leadership, suffering, and death traditions. Principal limitation: Paul is outside the pre-Ascension eleven, the two Jameses present sharply different causal records, and Peter’s and Paul’s deaths remain entangled with Nero’s political violence, making the quartet evidentially nonuniform. Live burden: Horn must establish for each individual a firsthand resurrection belief, sustained public witness, foreseeable cost, and meaningful option to withdraw before the cases can reinforce one another or support extrapolation. Locked score: 84 recognizes a focused and historically serious core argument, reduced for assembling unlike witness categories whose shared relevance is plausible but not sufficiently demonstrated.

moves.words: Paulogia accepts Acts as evidence that James son of Zebedee was killed but argues its brevity leaves the reason for his death historically unclear.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia correctly distinguishes the well-supported proposition that James son of Zebedee was killed from the stronger claim that he knowingly died rather than retract resurrection testimony, using the extreme brevity of Acts as decisive caution about motive. Principal limitation: Sparse narration does not positively favor a political or nonreligious explanation, and James’s leadership within a targeted movement supplies some contextual probability for religious hostility. Live burden: Horn must add evidence connecting execution to public resurrection witness and available withdrawal, whereas Paulogia needs only sustain causal underdetermination rather than establish a competing motive. Locked score: 88 reflects sharp burden discipline and a highly consequential source distinction, tempered because the critique sometimes presses documentary silence beyond what the surrounding movement context allows.

moves.words: Horn argues that Acts’ unembellished notice of James son of Zebedee looks less like a heroic Christian legend and therefore supports the death’s historicity.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn plausibly observes that Acts reports James son of Zebedee’s execution without a heroic speech, miraculous endurance, recantation drama, or devotional ornament, making the underlying death look less like elaborated martyr legend. Principal limitation: Narrative restraint can modestly support occurrence but cannot reveal Herod’s motive, James’s choices, or whether resurrection proclamation caused the killing, which are precisely the disputed elements. Live burden: Horn must confine the anti-embellishment inference to historicity unless independent evidence supplies the missing causal and volitional connections, while Paulogia should concede that terseness is not itself suspicious. Locked score: 80 credits a useful source-critical observation and responsive defense of historicity, but the middling result reflects its limited reach toward the sincerity conclusion that gives the episode argumentative importance.

moves.words: Horn combines Josephus with Christian traditions from Hegesippus and Clement to argue that James the brother of Jesus was killed after prominent Christian leadership.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn brings Josephus together with Christian material associated with Hegesippus and Clement, making James the brother of Jesus’s prominence and violent death considerably better attested than the fates of most original disciples. Principal limitation: The accounts differ in date, purpose, detail, and possible dependence, and their numerical plurality does not independently attest a shared persecutor motive, recantation opportunity, or final resurrection confession. Live burden: Horn must isolate what Josephus securely establishes from later devotional additions and show why overlapping reports support death for Christian proclamation rather than merely identity, leadership, and execution. Locked score: 84 reflects strong evidential breadth and appropriate attention to an unusually documented figure, discounted because the attestation is substantially firmer for the death than for the sincerity-testing mechanism inferred from it.

moves.words: Paulogia argues that James the brother of Jesus could have been eliminated through factional politics, so execution alone does not establish ideological martyrdom.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia identifies a historically grounded causal alternative by locating James’s death within a disputed exercise of high-priestly power during a gubernatorial transition, rather than assuming a formal choice between recantation and execution. Principal limitation: Ancient political authority and religious enforcement were intertwined, so factional opportunity does not exclude hostility toward James’s Christian teaching and cannot independently identify the decisive motive. Live burden: Horn must show that resurrection proclamation materially explains the accusation and sentence, while Paulogia must preserve uncertainty without presenting political elimination as proven by the same sparse narrative. Locked score: 85 rewards a relevant contextual complication that directly weakens an apologetic inference, with calibration below the strongest cards because it establishes credible underdetermination rather than a well-supported affirmative reconstruction.

moves.words: Horn infers that an accusation of breaking Jewish law fits punishment for leading Israel toward worship centered on the risen Jesus better than James’s reputed Torah observance.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn offers an intelligible explanation for why a leader remembered as Torah observant could nevertheless be accused as a lawbreaker, proposing that directing Israel toward the risen Jesus might attract a religiously serious charge and stoning. Principal limitation: Josephus never specifies that offense, the portrait of James’s observance comes through contested traditions, and several legally or politically intelligible accusations remain available. Live burden: Horn must corroborate the proposed connection between lawbreaking and resurrection preaching before the accusation can authenticate James’s witness, while Paulogia need not discover the exact alternative charge. Locked score: 80 reflects a contextually informed and candidly acknowledged inference, held down by dependence on silence and by the substantial distance between a plausible charge and the particular historical causation the argument requires.

moves.words: Horn reads Tacitus as indicating that Christians were punished not merely for Rome’s fire but also for their hated identity and alleged hostility toward humankind.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn carefully notes that Tacitus does not portray every Christian punishment as a simple arson conviction, since hated Christian identity and the accusation of hostility toward humankind figure in the described persecution. Principal limitation: Tacitus names neither Peter nor Paul, records no individual examination, and provides no evidence that resurrection testimony or refusal to recant determined either leader’s fate under Nero. Live burden: Horn must connect the general environment of belief-directed hostility to identifiable choices and escape opportunities for particular witnesses, while Paulogia must allow that Christian identity itself could create genuine danger. Locked score: 85 recognizes a strong correction to an overly simple scapegoat account and responsible textual use, moderated because the passage establishes dangerous context much more securely than the individualized sincerity test under debate.

moves.words: Paulogia argues that Nero’s need for conspicuous scapegoats could make Peter’s or Paul’s recantation irrelevant, weakening death as evidence that either voluntarily maintained testimony.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia shows that Nero’s political need for conspicuous victims could make the private conviction or last-minute denial of prominent Christians irrelevant, directly challenging the assumed inference from execution to voluntary steadfastness. Principal limitation: This remains an undocumented reconstruction of Peter’s and Paul’s treatment, and political scapegoating could coexist with ideological hostility, ordinary interrogation, or opportunities to disengage earlier. Live burden: Horn must provide case-specific reason to believe recantation, sacrifice, flight, or withdrawal would probably have prevented punishment; Paulogia need only show that an effective escape route is unestablished. Locked score: 84 rewards a potent challenge to the central causal mechanism, while withholding higher marks because its alternative is plausible from Tacitus’s framing but cannot reconstruct the leaders’ actual arrests or final options.

moves.words: Horn insists that historical reasoning must compare probabilities rather than halt whenever several possible explanations can be imagined for persecution or death.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn correctly insists that historical inquiry must compare evidential probabilities rather than stop whenever several conceivable explanations can be listed, using Tacitus and Pliny to demand disciplined evaluation of actual ancient practices. Principal limitation: General appeals to probability cannot overcome temporal, regional, and procedural differences between Trajan’s administration and Nero’s exceptional crisis, nor can they supply missing evidence about particular apostles. Live burden: Horn must state why each comparison transfers and assign transparent weight to it; Paulogia must ground alternatives sufficiently to reduce probability instead of relying on bare logical possibility. Locked score: 87 reflects excellent methodological discipline and a responsive correction to indiscriminate agnosticism, slightly reduced because the principle is stronger than Horn’s specific comparative application across substantially different historical settings.

moves.words: Paulogia emphasizes that Roman treatment of Christians varied across cities and decades, preventing later procedures from being assumed for Nero’s Rome or every apostolic setting.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia accurately emphasizes that Roman treatment of Christians varied across rulers, cities, officials, and decades, preventing Trajan’s documented procedures from being assumed for Nero’s Rome or every setting associated with apostolic risk. Principal limitation: Administrative variation does not establish that recantation was unavailable in the relevant cases, and recurring patterns from other evidence may still support carefully limited comparative inference. Live burden: Horn must justify transfers between periods and jurisdictions person by person, while Paulogia must calibrate uncertainty without treating nonuniformity as proof that meaningful danger or escape opportunities never existed. Locked score: 88 rewards a historically essential qualification that blocks false procedural uniformity, moderated only because it constrains extrapolation more decisively than it supplies an alternative account of particular leaders’ treatment.

moves.words: Horn reframes the argument around leaders who continued public association despite knowing that Christian identification could bring mob violence, arrest, or death before any formal recantation scene.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn improves the sincerity argument by shifting attention from undocumented courtroom recantation scenes to leaders who continued visible Christian activity after warnings, beatings, arrests, or circulating knowledge that identification could bring violence. Principal limitation: General awareness of danger does not establish every unnamed apostle’s later activity, perceived exposure, practical alternatives, or persistence, and people can accept risk for motives besides firsthand conviction. Live burden: Horn must document conduct and foreseeable cost person by person, then connect persistence specifically to resurrection belief; Paulogia must address anticipatory exposure separately from doubts about execution procedure. Locked score: 88 reflects a historically more defensible and dialectically responsive formulation, with a measured deduction because its force remains concentrated in documented leaders rather than the entire apostolic roster.

moves.words: Paulogia asks whether an available escape through denial would weaken the claim that ordinary participants incurred serious risk simply by joining or preaching within the movement.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia exposes a genuine tension between describing lethal participation costs and also treating denial or sacrifice as a practical route by which accused Christians might escape punishment. Principal limitation: Recantation could still involve detention, humiliation, destroyed relationships, lost leadership, and uncertain official acceptance, so its availability would reduce rather than eliminate the evidential cost of participation. Live burden: Horn must establish how accessible and effective recantation was in each setting and why its social costs meaningfully tested sincerity; Paulogia must avoid assuming a universal, costless escape. Locked score: 83 rewards a pointed internal challenge that improves calibration of the risk claim, but the score remains moderate because the argument initially understates substantial nonlethal consequences and lacks person-specific evidence about actual recantation options.

moves.words: Horn argues that recanting could preserve life while destroying a leader’s standing, exposing deception, and producing lasting exclusion within a community that remembered apostasy.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn shows that surviving persecution through denial could still expose deception, destroy a leader’s standing, and produce durable exclusion, supporting sincerity even when recantation might preserve physical life. Principal limitation: His named-defector texts and much later Donatist controversy do not securely establish first-century consequences, and Peter’s or Paul’s favorable reputation cannot be distributed to silent members of the eleven. Live burden: Horn must demonstrate that comparable sanctions were expected by each relevant person and that remembered steadfastness is historically probative rather than retrospective idealization; Paulogia must weigh real social losses. Locked score: 88 reflects a strong and necessary answer to the supposed cost-free escape card, slightly reduced because the most concrete institutional analogy is temporally remote and the evidence remains markedly stronger for selected leaders.

moves.words: Paulogia replies that people facing severe punishment may accept exclusion or lost status, so a chance to recant still reduces the evidential force of prior risk-taking.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia reasonably argues that a person confronting torture or execution may accept exclusion and lost status, so an available denial still substantially lowers the cost of earlier participation even when it is socially painful. Principal limitation: The analogy with collaborators abandoning companions does not measure early Christian honor, livelihood, attachment, or the credibility damage of admitting fabrication, while some adherents demonstrably prefer those losses to recantation. Live burden: Horn must establish the stakes and later conduct of unnamed witnesses; Paulogia must provide more than abstract human defeasibility if recantation is to diminish documented endurance. Locked score: 82 credits a useful corrective to Horn’s reputational emphasis, but its evidential grounding and cultural specificity are limited, leaving it more effective as a caution than as a decisive counterexplanation.

moves.words: Horn compares lesser-known apostles with close associates of Martin Luther King Jr., arguing that knowingly remaining near a threatened leader can indicate sincere commitment without constant public speeches.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn’s comparison with close associates of a threatened civil-rights leader usefully shows that sustained, visible proximity to a dangerous cause may evidence commitment even when no individual speech or formal martyrdom is preserved. Principal limitation: Modern photographs, reporting, and organizational records establish those associates and their exposure far better than ancient sources establish each apostle’s later location, visibility, duration of service, or recognized danger. Live burden: Horn must prove the continuing association before the analogy can interpret its significance, while Paulogia should acknowledge that documented non-speaking participation can still carry evidential weight. Locked score: 83 reflects an illuminating conceptual analogy that broadens relevant conduct, moderated because the comparison assumes the very historical association disputed for most unnamed disciples and therefore cannot independently supply it.

moves.words: Paulogia answers that the analogy fails unless evidence first establishes that each alleged apostle remained visibly connected to the movement after Jesus’s death and early Jerusalem episodes.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia identifies the missing prerequisite in Horn’s analogy: before risk can be inferred from association, the record must establish that each alleged apostle remained visibly connected to the movement after Jesus’s death and the earliest Jerusalem episodes. Principal limitation: Collective traditions, stable group identity, and early shared activity provide some positive evidence, so absence of individual biographies should reduce confidence rather than erase association entirely. Live burden: Horn must distinguish remembered membership from sustained hazardous service for every person; Paulogia need not prove departure but must preserve graded probabilities where collective evidence applies. Locked score: 90 reflects exceptionally precise burden analysis aimed at the argument’s hidden premise, with only a limited deduction because it sometimes describes the evidential cutoff more categorically than the surviving group testimony warrants.

moves.words: Horn clarifies that willingness to suffer addresses whether witnesses sincerely reported perceived resurrection experiences, not whether those experiences objectively verify a bodily resurrection.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn sharply confines the martyrdom reasoning to whether alleged witnesses sincerely reported perceived resurrection experiences, thereby excluding irrelevant comparisons with later martyrs who inherited beliefs and avoiding a direct claim that suffering proves bodily resurrection. Principal limitation: Sincerity alone cannot determine an experience’s independence, sensory content, physicality, or cause, and Paul does not occupy exactly the same experiential category as pre-Ascension disciples. Live burden: Horn must identify who personally claimed what and show why costly conduct authenticates that report; Paulogia should contest those links without requiring this argument to prove objective resurrection. Locked score: 92 reflects outstanding conceptual precision, responsiveness, and protection against a common straw objection, with the small deduction reserved for unresolved variation among the firsthand claims grouped together.

moves.words: Paulogia grants Paul’s sincerity while classifying his post-Ascension experience with later visions, which cannot independently guarantee the same bodily event allegedly encountered by earlier disciples.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia grants Paul’s sincerity while distinguishing a post-Ascension appearance from an alleged encounter with a recently revived body, preventing Paul’s costly conviction from automatically corroborating the same experiential proposition attributed to earlier disciples. Principal limitation: This distinction affects what Paul verifies, not whether he sincerely believed Jesus appeared, so it has limited force against Horn’s explicitly narrowed sincerity claim. Live burden: Horn must specify the shared proposition on which Paul and the eleven count together; Paulogia must avoid using categorical difference to discount Paul’s unusually strong sincerity evidence. Locked score: 84 recognizes a significant evidential distinction and an intellectually honest concession, reduced because part of the response addresses resurrection verification beyond the immediate debate over sincere proclamation.

moves.words: Horn challenges a proposed trauma-based explanation for Paul because Paul’s letters do not report guilt or distress over his earlier persecution before his conversion experience.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn correctly demands case-specific evidence for a psychological account, noting that Paul’s letters describe persecution without reporting pre-conversion grief, intrusive memories, or trauma symptoms that would anchor the proposed mechanism. Principal limitation: Ancient letters are not clinical autobiographies, and absence of self-description cannot show that delayed psychological reactions were impossible or even improbable. Live burden: Paulogia must either support the trauma proposal comparatively or keep it peripheral, while Horn cannot treat one weak naturalistic explanation’s failure as confirmation of an objective appearance. Locked score: 89 reflects a forceful and properly targeted evidential objection that secures an explicit concession, moderated because it defeats an unsupported proposal more successfully than it advances Horn’s own historical explanation.

moves.words: Paulogia expressly concedes that his post-traumatic-stress suggestion for Paul is speculative and unsupported by explicit testimony, limiting it to a possible naturalistic mechanism.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia answers directly that the trauma proposal is complete speculation without explicit textual support, while clarifying the limited psychological point that delayed symptoms need not involve remorse during the precipitating conduct. Principal limitation: A mechanism that is merely psychologically possible and unattested in the individual case contributes almost nothing to comparative historical probability or explanation of Paul’s reported experience. Live burden: Paulogia must add evidence or withdraw the proposal from substantive comparison, and Horn must avoid converting that withdrawal into positive supernatural evidence. Locked score: 90 rewards unusually clear self-correction, accurate limitation, and refusal to overclaim after challenge, with a modest deduction because the original conjecture was under-evidenced and the concession leaves no developed alternative account.

moves.words: Horn combines Acts’ collective descriptions of apostolic testimony and punishment with Paul’s statement that “I or they” preached the received resurrection message.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn joins Acts’ collective descriptions of apostolic testimony, punishment, and continued teaching with Paul’s distinction between “I” and “they” preaching the received resurrection message, creating genuine convergence beyond Peter alone. Principal limitation: Collective grammar may summarize representative leadership, Paul does not enumerate all eleven, and neither source supplies continuous individual histories or equal exposure for every member. Live burden: Horn must establish independence, intended referents, distributive scope, and chronological continuity; Paulogia must explain why the sources establish less than a recognizable cohort of earlier proclaimers. Locked score: 88 reflects substantial cumulative evidence and effective textual synthesis, tempered because the move from group-level proclamation to person-specific hazardous persistence remains the central unresolved inference.

moves.words: Paulogia argues that Acts’ group portrait ends before reliable individual histories emerge, leaving most disciples’ later preaching, persistence, and exposure undocumented.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia accurately distinguishes evidence for early collective proclamation from evidence that every member continued hazardous public ministry across later decades, observing that Acts soon narrows its narrative attention to a few figures. Principal limitation: A change in narrative focus does not imply withdrawal, and the early collective scenes remain affirmative evidence of at least some shared activity rather than mere silence. Live burden: Horn must support continuity beyond the early episodes; Paulogia should preserve what those episodes establish and avoid treating later disappearance as evidence of departure. Locked score: 87 rewards a consequential chronological distinction and careful resistance to overextension, with a measured reduction because the argument establishes declining documentation more clearly than declining individual participation.

moves.words: Horn argues that “apostle” fundamentally denotes a messenger, with the eleven occupying a special eyewitness class, so continued apostolic identity implies public transmission of the message.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn gives the title “apostle” evidential content by explaining its basic messenger sense and its specialized application to longstanding disciples regarded as resurrection witnesses, making entirely private inactivity less congruent with the remembered role. Principal limitation: A role title can preserve ideal status after conduct changes, and broader New Testament usage prevents identical duration, publicity, or danger from being inferred semantically for every bearer. Live burden: Horn must connect the designation to documented post-Easter actions by particular members; Paulogia should recognize its probabilistic relevance without accepting it as a biography. Locked score: 83 reflects a coherent semantic contribution that modestly supports public function, held below stronger evidence because nomenclature alone cannot establish continuous hazardous practice.

moves.words: Paulogia argues that Horn stacks uncertain steps from group membership to preaching, from preaching to danger, and from danger to sincere firsthand resurrection belief.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia isolates the argument’s cumulative vulnerability: uncertain transitions from membership to later preaching, from preaching to recognized danger, and from danger to sincerity about a particular firsthand experience can magnify uncertainty when applied to every apostle. Principal limitation: Historical reasoning necessarily chains inferences, and independent convergence can strengthen a conclusion even when no source explicitly records every intermediate step. Live burden: Horn must support and calibrate each transition rather than presenting their product as secure; Paulogia must challenge actual probabilities instead of rejecting inference or demanding modern documentation. Locked score: 90 reflects exceptionally strong structural diagnosis and burden control, with a small deduction because the warning becomes overstated whenever it treats inferential reasoning itself, rather than weakly supported links, as objectionable.

moves.words: Horn contends that Luke’s collective reports and Paul’s independent language in First Corinthians jointly support group preaching more strongly than either source would alone.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn shows that Luke’s collective apostolic reports and Paul’s independent “I or they” language converge on a preaching group associated with resurrection claims, giving the proposition broader support than either source supplies alone. Principal limitation: Neither text unambiguously enumerates all eleven, and collective grammar or pronouns can refer to representative proclaimers without distributing identical conduct and endurance to every remembered disciple. Live burden: Horn must establish source independence, intended membership, and distributive scope; Paulogia must explain why convergence fails to support at least some organized earlier proclamation. Locked score: 89 rewards a strong cumulative textual case and direct response to excessive silence-based skepticism, moderated because its best-supported conclusion concerns a cohort, not the complete individualized roster needed for Horn’s widest claim.

moves.words: Paulogia accepts that Paul’s letters connect him with Peter, James, and John but argues that evidence for named leaders cannot establish the conduct of seven or eight silent individuals.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia identifies the decisive evidential asymmetry between concrete meetings involving Peter, James, John, and Paul and the absence of comparable independent histories for Bartholomew, Matthew, and several other disciples. Principal limitation: Credible group testimony can support unnamed members without eleven separate biographies, so non-naming reduces confidence but does not make individual participation evidentially empty. Live burden: Horn must justify distributing representative-leader evidence across the bounded eleven; Paulogia needs only show that confidence should decline for silent individuals, not prove that anyone abandoned the movement. Locked score: 92 reflects a highly precise challenge to quantifier scope, excellent preservation of the proper burden, and strong source discrimination, with minimal deduction because collective evidence retains more residual force than the rhetoric occasionally concedes.

moves.words: Paulogia says the unnamed disciples’ disappearance from reliable history is compatible with continued ministry, quiet membership, fishing, withdrawal, or later appropriation of their names.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia correctly observes that the later silence about most disciples is compatible with continued ministry, private membership, return to ordinary work, withdrawal, or continued symbolic use of their names, preventing one outcome from being assumed. Principal limitation: These possibilities are not equally probable, and early collective activity plus stable group memory provides some positive evidence against treating later status as wholly unconstrained. Live burden: Horn must produce continuity evidence that narrows the range; Paulogia must keep illustrative possibilities hypothetical and incorporate the evidence preceding disappearance. Locked score: 86 reflects a disciplined defense of underdetermination and a useful check on narrative completion, reduced because multiplying possibilities does less evidential work than comparing their relative fit and can slide toward the agnosticism Horn appropriately criticizes.

moves.words: Horn argues that early Christians named defectors as warnings, so conspicuous abandonment by original apostles would likely have been noticed rather than silently concealed.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn develops a plausible expectation that repudiation by a foundational eyewitness would be memorable and polemically useful, supporting continuity through comparison with Christian texts that explicitly name defectors as warnings. Principal limitation: Partisan sources preserve information selectively, their dating and authorship may be disputed, and quiet withdrawal need not produce the conspicuous repudiation that Horn’s expectation requires. Live burden: Horn must establish community knowledge, incentives, and reliable transmission before silence can support all eleven; Paulogia must acknowledge that visible defection by a major witness would probably matter. Locked score: 82 credits a relevant argument from expected evidence and an apt internal comparison, while the moderate score reflects substantial preservation bias and the inability of silence to prove lifelong preaching or dangerous persistence.

moves.words: Horn challenges a picture of an initially disorganized movement, citing early elders, planted churches, apostolic connections, and the Jerusalem council as structures capable of tracking leaders.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn counters a picture of total early disorganization by citing elders, connected church plants, hierarchical language, apostolic links, and the Jerusalem council, showing that information about prominent leaders could circulate through functioning networks. Principal limitation: Organizational capacity varied by place and time and does not establish that every original disciple remained active, observable, or accurately represented within those networks. Live burden: Horn must connect institutional structure to person-specific continuity evidence; Paulogia should not explain silence by assuming atomized communities when early coordination is independently attested. Locked score: 78 reflects a useful contextual correction with real background relevance, but its comparatively low result recognizes that capacity to track leaders is several inferential steps removed from proof of each apostle’s hazardous activity.

moves.words: Horn concludes that the strongest sincerity argument is continued proclamation under foreseeable mob violence or persecution, rather than universal execution after explicit recantation offers.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn’s concluding formulation aligns the sincerity inference with the best available evidence by emphasizing continued proclamation amid foreseeable beatings, mob action, arrest, and possible death instead of requiring universal execution after explicit recantation offers. Principal limitation: Expected suffering remains evidentially powerful only where public conduct, awareness, alternatives, persistence, and the relevant firsthand belief are established, and those conditions differ sharply among individuals. Live burden: Horn must apply the test person by person without universalizing the strongest cases; Paulogia must explain documented costly persistence among supported leaders. Locked score: 89 reflects a mature, responsive, and historically proportionate refinement that captures genuine evidential force, slightly reduced because the all-eleven conclusion still outruns the individually documented instances satisfying its own conditions.

moves.words: Paulogia insists that a positive claim about eleven individuals requires evidence covering all eleven, especially when their alleged sincerity becomes a foundation for further resurrection arguments.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia states the central quantificational burden clearly: evidence for sincere believers and several named leaders cannot alone establish the positive claim that every one of the eleven maintained hazardous resurrection proclamation. Principal limitation: Universal propositions can sometimes follow from credible collective reports without separate biographies, so requiring modern-style individual files would impose anachronistic evidential standards. Live burden: Horn must show that collective sources genuinely quantify over the bounded eleven during the relevant period; Paulogia must proportion skepticism to ancient evidence rather than demand impossibly explicit documentation. Locked score: 94 reflects the debate’s strongest burden analysis, exceptional scope precision, and direct exposure of the inferential gap, with only a slight reservation for occasional language that undervalues legitimate group-level testimony.

moves.words: Paulogia proposes that only one early witness plus Paul need have sincere experiences for resurrection belief to spread, reducing the explanatory need for eleven independent hazardous testimonies.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia offers a parsimonious possibility in which one early sincere visionary experience and Paul’s later experience can generate a growing movement, demonstrating that Christian expansion does not logically require eleven independent hazardous testimonies. Principal limitation: The scenario remains schematic and does not adequately explain early group formulas, multiple named leaders, collective Acts traditions, or the particular emergence of appearance claims in their recorded forms. Live burden: Paulogia must compare a developed narrative against the entire dataset rather than cite minimal sufficiency; Horn must identify evidence that specifically requires multiple independent experiences. Locked score: 74 recognizes a relevant alternative that changes the explanatory landscape, but its low score reflects underdevelopment, limited source engagement, and much weaker historical specification than its confidently stated downstream implications require.

moves.words: Horn urges both sides to construct complete historical narratives and compare how well each explains the evidence instead of treating isolated uncertainties as decisive.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Horn closes with a sound comparative principle: rival historical accounts should be assessed by total explanatory fit, assumptions, scope, and treatment of contrary evidence rather than allowing isolated gaps or possibilities to decide the outcome. Principal limitation: A detailed narrative can manufacture apparent coherence when unsupported connective assumptions are mistaken for evidence, and supernatural explanations require clearly stated comparative standards. Live burden: Horn must identify distinctive predictions without filling silence with apostolic continuity; Paulogia must develop his minimal account enough to explain collective traditions and named witnesses. Locked score: 88 reflects excellent methodological synthesis and a constructive path beyond piecemeal objection, tempered because the debate does not actually complete the demanding comparative analysis that the principle recommends.

strengths: Horn narrows the martyrdom argument to unequal, person-specific evidence instead of defending every later apostolic death tradition.
He correctly separates sincerity from objective resurrection truth and identifies foreseeable suffering before arrest as the stronger evidential test.
He combines Acts, Paul, Josephus, Tacitus, and community context while repeatedly acknowledging where motive or continuity remains inferential.

blunders.text: Horn sometimes moves too quickly from collective apostolic language to continuous hazardous activity by every member of the eleven.
His use of later Roman procedures and later church discipline does not securely reconstruct Nero’s decisions or first-century recantation costs.

strengths: Paulogia consistently separates evidence of death, motive, opportunity to recant, public preaching, and sincere firsthand experience.
He grants strong points, including Horn’s nuance and Paul’s sincerity, while preserving the narrower burden concerning every original witness.
He exposes cumulative uncertainty when sparse individual evidence is expanded through group labels, silence, and analogies into a universal conclusion.

blunders.text: Paulogia’s trauma account of Paul is expressly speculative and offers no case-specific evidence capable of improving comparative probability.
His minimal-experiences scenario remains too schematic to explain the early collective formulas, named leaders, and precise development of group claims.

finalArgument.thesis: The evidence can conditionally support sincere hazardous proclamation by all original witnesses, but confidence must be proportioned to whether bounded group references genuinely include each member.
premises: Acts presents a bounded apostolic group collectively testifying, accepting punishment, and continuing to teach after an explicit prohibition.
Paul later distinguishes his preaching from that of earlier appearance recipients, providing a potential chronological bridge beyond the earliest Jerusalem episode.
Named leaders supply independent anchors showing that resurrection proclamation and serious personal cost were not merely literary abstractions within the movement.

If the collective references intentionally encompass the original eleven, shared warning and publicly observable group conduct make undisclosed individual repudiation less likely during those episodes.

The inference weakens for later continuity because surviving sources cease tracking most individuals, so universal lifelong endurance cannot be assigned the confidence warranted for the early bounded episodes.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, all-original-witness sincerity is defensible as a calibrated inference for the early collective activity only if the group referents are established, while later hazardous persistence remains strongest for named leaders.

newArguments.title: Mutual-observation constraint
newArguments.text: A genuinely bounded episode of collective warning, punishment, and resumed teaching would create mutual observation among participants: each member’s compliance or repudiation could affect the group’s public credibility. If Acts reliably describes the original eleven rather than representative leaders, that social structure makes fabricated unanimity harder to sustain during the episode. This adds a verification mechanism beyond mere exposure to danger, although it cannot establish later careers or apply to anyone whose presence in the bounded group remains uncertain.

newArguments.title: Chronological triangulation
newArguments.text: Acts locates collective proclamation early, while Paul’s later “I or they” formulation attributes preaching to earlier appearance recipients in a community-facing letter. If those referents overlap substantially with the original witness group, the two temporal vantage points reduce the probability that every unnamed disciple immediately disappeared after Acts. The inference is conditional on referent identity and source independence, but it adds a chronological bridge rather than simply repeating that danger existed or that apostasy went unreported.

finalArgument.thesis: The all-eleven sincerity claim remains underdetermined because collective references do not establish equivalent identity, continuity, danger, or counterfactual choice for each original witness.
premises: A death or punishment supports sincerity only when the relevant testimony, persecutor motive, and an effective opportunity to avoid the cost are independently connected.

The clearest individual evidence concerns a few named leaders, while Paul’s post-Ascension experience supports sincerity without independently verifying the same kind of encounter attributed to the eleven.
Collective language may describe a real preaching cohort yet remain compatible with representative speech, changing membership, unequal participation, or a limited early episode.
Apparent convergence between sources may overstate support when later narratives and communal traditions depend on the same inherited group memory.
Because Roman responses varied and Nero may have valued Christian identity as a scapegoating category, punishment does not uniformly reveal what recantation or withdrawal would have changed.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, sincerity is well supported for Paul and several leaders, but a universal claim about the original eleven requires person-distributing evidence and counterfactual cost conditions that the surviving record does not securely provide.

newArguments.title: Dependence ceiling
newArguments.text: Several statements can appear cumulative while tracing back to one community-level representation of “the apostles.” Before multiplying confidence, the argument must ask whether Acts’ collective scenes, Paul’s inherited formula, and later continuity assumptions independently identify the same individuals or merely repeat a shared category. If dependence is substantial, agreement supports the existence of an apostolic proclamation tradition but places a ceiling on person-by-person conclusions. This adds a source-correlation problem distinct from the ordinary complaint that individual biographies are missing.

newArguments.title: Counterfactual cost test
newArguments.text: Costly behavior evidences sincerity only when abandoning the disputed belief would probably have changed the cost. A mob attacking a recognized leader, or Nero selecting a prominent Christian scapegoat, might punish identity and political usefulness regardless of a private retraction. Each case therefore needs a counterfactual comparison: what action was available, would authorities have recognized it, and would it likely have prevented harm? This test explains why genuine suffering can coexist with weak evidential force about maintained resurrection testimony.

noveltyMap.explanation: Adds an explicit conditional route to the all-original-witness scope: bounded collective referents can distribute early sincerity evidence, while later continuity receives lower person-specific confidence.

Introduces mutual observation as a social verification mechanism: within a genuinely bounded punished group, individual compliance or repudiation would be visible to fellow participants and affect credibility.
Uses the temporal separation between Acts’ early episode and Paul’s later community-facing formulation to create a conditional continuity bridge, rather than inferring continuity from silence.
Integrates identity, source dependence, and counterfactual cost into the universal burden, preserving strong named cases while explaining why their support cannot automatically distribute.
Adds a correlation check: apparently convergent references may repeat one inherited apostolic category, limiting how much agreement increases confidence about separate individuals.
Adds a decision-theoretic counterfactual: suffering supports sincerity only to the extent that abandoning the relevant testimony would probably have prevented the cost.
